name: High cholesterol
tagline: What the numbers mean for your heart.
sources: Lipid and Atherosclerosis Society of South Africa

what_is_it.heading: Cholesterol in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Cholesterol is a fatty substance your body needs to build cells and make hormones. The problem is the type and the amount — too much of the wrong kind builds up in artery walls and causes heart attacks and strokes.
paragraphs: Your liver makes most of your cholesterol. Some also comes from food, especially animal products. LDL ('bad') cholesterol carries fat into the artery walls. HDL ('good') cholesterol clears it away. The balance matters.

Some people have inherited high cholesterol (familial hypercholesterolaemia) — their numbers are dangerously high from childhood, regardless of diet. This is the most under-diagnosed cause of early heart attacks. If a close relative had a heart attack before 60, get checked.

items.headline: Silent
items.body: High cholesterol has no symptoms. You only know from a blood test.

items.headline: Main cause
items.body: Of heart attacks and most strokes. LDL is the strongest modifiable risk factor we know.

items.headline: Genes count
items.body: Familial high cholesterol affects roughly 1 in 200 people — many never know until a heart attack.

items.headline: Statins work
items.body: Decades of evidence: statins cut heart attacks and strokes by a third or more in people at risk.

pull_quote.text: Cholesterol is not just a lifestyle problem. Thin, fit, healthy-eating people can still have dangerously high cholesterol from inherited genes. Get tested — especially if anyone in your family had an early heart attack.
pull_quote.source: Lipid and Atherosclerosis Society of South Africa

signs.heading: What you might notice
signs.lede: For most people: nothing. High cholesterol does its damage silently over decades. The only way to know is a blood test.

items.title: No everyday symptoms
items.description: Cholesterol does not make you feel anything. The first sign for many people is a heart attack or stroke in their forties or fifties.

items.title: Very high genetic levels
items.description: Yellow patches around the eyelids or fatty bumps on the tendons (Achilles, knuckles) can be signs of familial cholesterol. A grey ring around the iris before age 45 is another.

items.title: Family history is the clue
items.description: Parents, siblings, or grandparents with heart attacks or strokes before 60 — especially before 50 — strongly suggests genetic high cholesterol.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Only overweight people get high cholesterol.
items.fact: Thin people get high cholesterol too — often from genetics. Body shape is not a reliable signal. Only a blood test is.
Dietary cholesterol from eggs has a small effect on blood cholesterol for most people. Saturated fats and trans fats matter more.
Large studies have not found a link. Statins occasionally cause muscle aches — tell your clinic if so, alternatives exist.

items.myth: If I exercise, I do not need to worry about diet.
items.fact: Exercise mostly raises HDL (good cholesterol) but has only a small effect on LDL. Diet, weight, and medication matter more for LDL.

prevention.heading: How to lower your numbers
prevention.lede: Cholesterol responds well to a combination of diet, weight, exercise, and medication where needed. Most people can move their numbers significantly within months.

items.title: Mediterranean-style eating
items.description: Vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, fish, olive oil. Limit red meat, butter, full-cream dairy, fried foods, and processed meats.

items.title: Cut trans fats entirely
items.description: Hidden in many baked goods, margarines, and fried takeaways. Read labels — anything with 'partially hydrogenated oils' is out.

items.title: Move every day
items.description: Exercise raises HDL (the good kind) and helps weight. Even brisk walking 30 minutes a day makes a measurable difference.

items.title: Statins where indicated
items.description: If your risk is high, or you have familial cholesterol, statins are the most effective treatment we have. Free at clinics.

items.title: Get a lipid panel
items.description: A simple fasting blood test measures total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides. Free at every government clinic from age 40 — or earlier with family history.

items.title: Know your numbers
items.description: Write them down. LDL under 3.0 is generally the goal — under 1.8 if you already have heart disease or diabetes. Targets are personal — ask your clinic.

items.title: If high — start with food and movement
items.description: Most people can drop LDL by 10–15% with diet and exercise alone. Give it three to six months before assuming medication is needed.

items.title: If medication is recommended — start it
items.description: Statins work best taken every day, long term. Skipping doses cancels most of the benefit. Side effects are uncommon and usually manageable.

items.title: Recheck every 12 months
items.description: Once stable, an annual lipid panel checks progress and adjusts treatment if needed. Bring previous results to compare.

get_help.heading: Where to start
get_help.lede: Cholesterol care is free at South African public clinics. The hardest part is getting the first test — once you have a number, the path forward is clear.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every clinic offers free cholesterol testing and free statins where prescribed
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
